doc.title: Dave Frishberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Placing songs and writing for his own voice
summary: He now writes mainly for himself to sing, so his songs suit his limited voice, unlike Bob Dorough's.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You’ve got new songs in the can for —
I have some that I haven’t recorded yet. And I have some brand new ones, yeah. So I wouldn’t call them in the can.
No they’re in the trunk or whatever you call it, the repository of songs. Yeah there are some ready to be used.
What’s it like to place songs these days, or do you have a reputation enough that—

Well I’m getting a reputation now that singers look for my work because they pick up on new songs really quickly. My song “Sideman” was covered almost immediately by two female singers, which I thought was kind of odd but gratifying. But most of the songs I
use myself, I just sing them, record them, and then I do my act and that’s my ammunition you know. I mean I’m writing them now mainly for myself to sing, which is fine.

Yeah. But number one it means they may not be covered a lot, and number two it means too that they’re going to be of a certain character which doesn’t require a great voice. And that dimension shapes my song to a certain degree. There’s not many of them that are ariose or that display the voice. So placing songs with singers is often — it has to do with giving the singer something that he or she will be able to sing. That’s what singers want. A lot of singers, that’s why they’re singers, right?
Right. Because they’ve got the instrument.

But when I write I’m writing according to the limitations of my own vocal ability. The song is not going to be that, they’re not going to display great singing, nor are they going to rely on long and loud held notes. You know what I mean?
Well that to some degree, to a big degree, shapes my songs. I bet Mose Allison would say the same thing. A lot of his songs are shaped by the way he sings.

Dorough on the other hand is a different kind of composer. He’s not bound by his own limitations. Dorough writes for a voice, and he’s a more thorough composer, a more versatile composer than I am. He writes a lot of songs that singers get their teeth into. “Love Came on Stealthy Fingers” and songs like that are ballads in demand by singers, and they use it to show off their voice. Carmen McRae and people like that, they bend it around. I don’t have a lot of songs like that.
